title: The Jazztone reissue mix-up and Leonard Feather's reunion album
summary: Jazztone mixed tracks from separate sessions; Leonard Feather reunited Kirby alumni to revive the sound; they plan to write Feather and Bethlehem.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: And then of course, the album that came out later which titled Flow Gently Sweet Rhythm, includes quite a few selections -- vocals -- that I had done.
Now we're talking about the reissue that was -- that came out on the Jazztone label, which is an album in your possession.
Right.

Now, it appears to me that what had happened is, I had recorded some of these things on a previous session. I don't even know what the label was or we recorded them for. And I believed that what happened here is, when they issued the album under the Jazztone series, they probably gathered up some of these things that I had recorded previously, and put them in the album and called that Flow Gently Sweet Rhythm.
Incidentally, the number of this album is Jazztone J1229, just to clarify.
Yeah.
Well, it's pretty obvious what happened

here, because there are some other tunes that are listed here that don't appear in the album that I recall as having recorded them at the time.

So, what they must have done was selected "Barbara Allen" or "Brown Bird Singing," "Jackie Boy," "Loch Lomond," "Oh No, John" and "Raggle Taggle Gypsies," and included them in that album that came out as Flow Gently Sweet Rhythm.
Yeah. Now the first few of those that you mentioned were just recorded with a trio.
Um hum.
Under the direction of Dick Hyman.
Right.
Harpsichord and organ, I think.
Right.
And the other three are by -- the last three that you mentioned are by a pick-up group which is a slightly lesser approximation of the Kirby sextet.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Well --
With Hilton Jefferson on alto.
Yeah. That's who I was trying to mention. Hilton Jefferson. Now those were the selections that were recorded on another date, not necessarily for Period -- I don't even know the company.
You said you thought it might be --
Prestige.
Prestige.

Yes, but I'm not sure. But when I see these other titles listed here -- "All Sweet Mystery of Life," "Turtle Dove" and "I Didn't Know About You," "I'm Coming Virginia," "St. Louis Blues," "When Your Love Has Gone" -- I identified them as the date in which Hilton Jefferson and Oscar Pettiford and O.C. Johnson were on this tape.
I've never heard these -- an album if it was ever released, with these songs on it. So
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
therefore, I never knew what happened to it.

Well that goes back to what we were saying last time. That it's absolutely incredible that an artist goes out and cuts an album, or cuts a pair of sides in the 78 days, and doesn't receive a copy. For me, that's absolutely outrageous.
Well, I don't know what happened. You not only get a copy, you never know what happens to the masters.
There's also that business side to it, too, in terms of...

When you consider that the Jazztone label, it was a subscription series. And I really don't know what system they used in compiling their records. I imagined that they would just take what they thought -- There's a possibility, because it was membership, they might've gotten some responses from their subscribers saying, 'we'd like to have this, we'd like to have that.' And they just put together an
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
album including all those things. And not necessarily by the same artist or the same group. I think they mixed them up.
And for a while -- and I'm sure that most of us never knew what happened to some of the things that we actually recorded.
That's the only way I can explain the mix-up here so far as the Flow Gently Sweet Rhythm album that finally came out, and as it was originally intended.
And when it finally showed up, it wound up with most of the vocals on there. I know that they weren't recorded at the time that we made that album.
And as I said before, I don't even know who we made these selections for.
Leonard Feather would know about that, because Leonard Feather was instrumental in assembling the musicians and getting these things together.
I think it had been maybe ten or fifteen years since there was any John Kirby or Maxine Sullivan

material out. So I think this was an effort on Leonard Feather's part to bring to the listening audience the attention that there was a John Kirby and a Maxine Sullivan.
That is, they recorded the recording -- the people who buy records. Because we were -- although we were busy,-- I mean, I was working in clubs and Kirby was working -- we just weren't making records.
And that's one of the reasons why Leonard got the group together and did the original Flow Gently Sweet Rhythm. It was supposed to be "Flow Gently Sweet Rhythm Revisited."

Incidentally, you're pretty convinced that was the first -- that session you're talking about now, the Flow Gently Sweet Rhythm one, with the reassembled Kirby Band -- was the first of these sessions that you recorded.
Oh, yes, definitely.
Recorded in 1955, not 1956.
Right.

As the Bruyninckx discography states.
Yes.
As a result of that, the Period records was interested in making an album of vocals. And it was Leonard's idea that we do the tribute to Andy Razaf.
And that was the -- It looks like that was the last of these that you recorded.
That's right.
Okay.
So it looks like we should, first of all, send off a letter to Leonard Feather to see if he can throw some light on the history of these sessions--
Yes, he would know, because he was responsible for these particular albums.
And also, I think I should contact Bethlehem Records, because they reissued some of these sides also, on an album called Complete

I don't know which of these -- all these titles appear on that album.
